name: Fortuna-Aurea
specific_features: Ancient dried river systems filled with precious metal deposits
description: Fortuna-Aurea gleams even from orbit, its surface shot through with gold-bearing quartz veins so rich and extensive that they catch the light of the distant sun and return it as a warm golden shimmer visible across the entire daylit hemisphere. The planet's geological history concentrated precious metals near the surface through billions of years of tectonic uplift and erosion, creating deposits of a richness that would have sparked wars on ancient Earth. Dried river systems carved when the planet still had liquid water are lined with alluvial gold deposits that lie exposed on the surface like offerings.

The thin atmosphere provides minimal protection from solar radiation and allows temperature extremes that make unshielded surface operations dangerous. Daytime in the equatorial regions can be tolerable in a standard environment suit, but nighttime temperatures plummet to ranges that stress equipment and endurance alike. The landscape is stark and beautiful in the way of all barren mineral worlds: clean lines, sharp shadows, and colors that range from the warm golds and coppers of the metal deposits to the cold grays and whites of the silicate bedrock.

The concentration of precious metals on Fortuna-Aurea exceeds anything found on naturally formed worlds in most star systems, and some geologists argue that the distribution is too convenient to be entirely natural. The gold-bearing veins follow patterns that could indicate artificial seeding, as though someone or something deliberately enriched this world's crust with specific elements. No other evidence of intervention has been found, but the geological models that would explain such concentration naturally require coincidences that strain credulity.

The discovery of Fortuna-Aurea triggered an economic crisis as the sheer volume of accessible precious metals threatened to destabilize commodity markets across multiple systems. Extraction rights are now tightly controlled by an interstellar regulatory body, with quotas designed to prevent market flooding. This has not prevented illegal mining operations, which maintain a persistent presence in the planet's more remote regions despite enforcement efforts. The irony is not lost on historians: a fortune beyond imagination, and the greatest challenge it presents is preventing it from making itself worthless.
